doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: His wife, his father's objection, and the musical family
summary: His father warns that marriage will keep him from piano; Marty lists his musically gifted relatives.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Now you having come from a musical family—
—can I assume that it was okay with your parents that you were going into this field?

As a matter of fact that’s funny you lead me into that. Because when I started going with my wife, I met my wife when we were both 18 years old. Obviously we were the same age just about. And we kept company for about two years. But after about a year, my father said to me “you can’t keep company with that girl.” I said, “why not?” He says, © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

“you’re planning on marrying her?” I said, “yeah.” He said, “well you can’t even think about that.” I said, “why?” He said, “she’s going to keep you away from studying the piano.” How would you like to have parents like that?
Well see you talk about a musical family?

My father played banjo and guitar, my mother played guitar, I had two brothers and two sisters. My brother Teddy was a piano player, my brother Andy was a drummer, both of my sisters were singers. My sister Margaret married a piano player named Shorty Allen, and my sister Josephine married a saxophone player named Bill Shine. Fantastic lead alto man. And my grandfather, my father’s father, played guitar, and my aunt — he was living with his daughter Josephine until he died, and she says the day he died he was sitting with the guitar in his hand, strumming the guitar. And then his father played guitar. So it went way back with the guitars and the music. And everybody, in fact when I started this project with the book, people used to say to me, “how many musicians in your generation, your family are musically inclined, or jazz or whatever.” I’d say, “I don’t know.” I started counting them and I got to 50 and I lost count. Because not only my family, but my mother’s side.
